extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, scientific method, and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for forming, testing, and interpreting inductive and syllogistic arguments; how to represent inferences, detect insufficiency of evidence, and handle multi-step 'trains of reasoning'.

rubrics_metrics.name: State inductions in their broadest generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalize from particular observations to a general theorem and express that theorem in its broadest form of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "This theorem it is extremely important to ascertain and declare, in its broadest form of generality" — giving the whole body of possible inferences from particulars a single general expression increases attention to the evidence and helps detect insufficiency (e.g., thinking in terms of 'all Roman emperors are just' would be falsified by Nero, Domitian). Use broad general statements so that any counter-instance reveals a defect in the premises by reductio ad impossibile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent reasoning in syllogistic form to verify validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Throw reasoning into the syllogistic form (induction to a general proposition followed by deduction) when there is any doubt about validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The syllogism "furnishes us with a mode in which those reasonings may always be represented, and which is admirably calculated, if they are inconclusive, to bring their inconclusiveness to light." Use syllogistic representation as a diagnostic tool — not because we must reason that way psychologically, but because it exposes gaps and hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major premise as assertion of sufficiency of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The major premise expresses that the instances adduced are sufficient to authorize the general conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt Whately's test: the major affirms that the chosen examples are an adequate sample to warrant inference to the whole class. Treat the major as the articulation of what the evidence is supposed to establish; if it is not true throughout its extent the inference fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor premise must establish resemblance between cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The minor premise affirms that the new case resembles known cases in the relevant respects (i.e., that it falls under the marks set by the generalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the minor sometimes needs independent proof (it may itself be an inferred conclusion). Example: 'Socrates is a man' asserts resemblance to observed, mortal persons; when resemblance is not directly observable, it requires further inductive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction establishes general propositions; deduction applies them
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the process of reasoning about unobserved cases as an induction to a general proposition followed by a deduction applying that proposition to particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although we may reason directly from particulars to particulars, for scientific assurance convert such reasoning into induction + deduction: first ascertain what attributes are marks of the target property, then test whether the particular has those marks. This separation is a security for correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer circuitous induction+deduction over straight analogy when doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: When arguing from known cases to an analogous unknown case, it is generally advantageous to first induce a general proposition from the known cases, then apply it to the unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach brings all parallel cases to view and increases likelihood of detecting insufficiency (e.g., rather than directly inferring Commodus will be just from particular impressions, derive the general rule and test it against counterexamples). Use the two-step route when there is any suspicion of error or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and analyze trains of reasoning (chains of inductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex inferences often require a series of inductions and syllogisms (a 'train of reasoning') to connect observations to a final unobserved conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: determining that a substance is poisonous may require one induction to identify it as arsenic and another to know arsenic is poisonous; political inferences may require several nested inductions. Treat each link as an independent induction grounded on particulars; examine each for sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use marks and marks-of-marks to identify class membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Define distinguishing marks by which cases may be recognized; where primary marks are not directly observable, use secondary marks (marks of marks) established by prior induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We often identify that a new case belongs to a class indirectly (a is a mark of b, b of c, etc.). Be explicit about the chain of marks used to bring a case within the scope of a generalization and test each step. In complex knowledge, several chains may converge to justify the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure each general proposition is true in its full extent
rubrics_metrics.description: Every general proposition used in a chain of reasoning must be true throughout the whole class it purports to cover if the argument is to be maintainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Every one of which propositions must be true in all its extent, if the argument is maintainable." If any fact fairly coming within the range of a general proposition is known or suspected to be otherwise, the original observations are insufficient; detecting such counterinstances undermines the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of consecrated insufficient generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations made on insufficient evidence tend to become entrenched and accepted by habit even after their evidentiary basis is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the countervailing inconvenience that inductive errors can harden into maxims; periodically revisit and revise generals when new evidence or remembered particulars contradict them. Don't confuse convenience of general language with epistemic security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish testing/verification from the inductive act itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Verifying that evidence is sufficient (a reflexive act of review) is not the same psychological operation as forming the inductive conclusion from evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that we draw conclusions from evidence itself, and only retrospectively test whether the evidence was sufficient. Formalizing reasoning into syllogistic/general propositions is a methodological step to make the testing likely to occur, but the testing is not the original induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use general formulæ for cognitive economy and consistent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulating general propositions allows one careful induction to be applied repeatedly without retaining bulky particulars in memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General propositions commit results to memory and provide 'commodious and immediately available' rules for future use. Their end is not truth per se but consistency and practical cognitive economy; they are indispensable for extensive reasoning though they must be kept subject to correction.
